note: 'Jesus replied, This is the most important: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One.' (Mark 12:29), quoting Deut 6:4. Matthew and Luke give the command without this sentence.
'Jesus declared, Love the Lord your God with all your heart' (Matt 22:37), quoting Deut 6:5 in answer to which is the great commandment.
'And the second is like it: Love your neighbor as yourself.' (Matt 22:39), quoting Lev 19:18.
'Jesus declared ... All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments' (Matt 22:37, 22:40).

The abridged record stands for the command as the gospels give it; this is the verse they are quoting. Deut 6:5 was named in that record's description and absent from its citations, so the trail ran out one step short of the source.

Implied for a structural reason rather than a doubtful one: an `abridged` record's name is deliberately not a quotation, so no cited verse can ever contain it and no relation touching one can satisfy the explicit test. That is a property of the kind, not a weakness in this edge.
'on these two commandments' (Matt 22:40) -- the first being the command quoted at v37.
'on these two commandments' (Matt 22:40) -- the second being the command quoted at v39.
'And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart' (Deut 6:5).
'and with all your mind' (Matt 22:37; Mark 12:30). **Not in Deut 6:5**, which the gospels are quoting. Both add it; Deuteronomy has might in that place.

Deut 6:5 has 'with all your strength' and Mark 12:30 'with all your strength'. The concept carries might as an alias, so this one edge covers both wordings -- which is the whole difficulty this record exists to show.
